implementation_notes: CompletableFuture is a Future any thread may complete, so the correlation table stores futures in a ConcurrentHashMap keyed by the id and the reply listener removes and completes the matching one. Deadline handling is in the JDK from Java 9 (orTimeout/completeOnTimeout) or via get(timeout, unit); JMS and AMQP already carry the value as JMSCorrelationID or correlation_id, and Spring AMQP's convertSendAndReceive performs this bookkeeping for you, so the hand-written table is for transports that carry no correlation of their own.
pitfalls: When two threads complete the same CompletableFuture only one succeeds, so completing a future whose entry was already removed silently drops the reply - decide explicitly whether that is the timeout path or a bug.
orTimeout fails the future with TimeoutException but does not cancel the outstanding request; the late reply then lands on a removed entry and must be discarded gracefully.
Removal and completion are not atomic by default: use remove(id) itself as the completion gate (as in the sketch) or computeIfPresent so a duplicate reply cannot be delivered twice.
Non-async CompletableFuture continuations run on whichever thread completed the future - the reply/IO thread - so heavy work or blocking I/O in a continuation must be handed to an executor.

variants.name: One virtual thread per request blocked on a hand-off queue (Java 21+)
variants.idiom_name: SynchronousQueue per request + virtual thread per call
variants.implementation_notes: With virtual threads (JEP 444, final in Java 21) the reason for the asynchronous future table largely disappears: give every outstanding request its own virtual thread parked on a blocking hand-off (a SynchronousQueue or a one-slot ArrayBlockingQueue) stored in the correlation map, and let the reply thread put the payload in. Blocking a virtual thread is cheap and nearly unlimited, so the code reads as an ordinary blocking call while scaling like the asynchronous style; keep the CompletableFuture variant on Java 8-17 or where the call chain is already reactive.
pitfalls: A virtual thread blocked inside a synchronized block or method pins its carrier (JEP 444); use ReentrantLock or block outside monitors so the carrier stays available.
poll() returning null is the timeout - do not confuse it with a legitimate null payload, and prefer a sentinel or Optional for empty results.
Do not funnel hand-offs through a fixed platform-thread pool or pool the virtual threads themselves: the variant relies on a fresh, cheap virtual thread per request.
put() on a SynchronousQueue blocks until a taker arrives, so the reply thread can stall; use offer with a timeout in the listener if the transport thread must never block.
